data.title: Russian attacks on Kyiv petrol stations kill two, Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia
data.description:
Russian attacks on Kyiv petrol stations kill two, Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia

Reuters
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 8:40 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Russian drone strike in Kyiv

1 of 6
Firefighters work at a site of an apartment building hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine September 11, 2026. REUTERS/Gleb Garanich

Sept 11 (Reuters) - Russia attacked two Kyiv petrol stations with jet-powered drones early on Friday, killing two people in an escalation of strikes that President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said were becoming "increasingly terrorist in nature."

Two more people were killed in Russian strikes in southeastern Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region and ‌in Kharkiv in the northeast, according to the regions' governors.

Ukraine also carried out drone attacks on Russia, killing two people in the Tula region ‌overnight and one on Friday in the Kursk region, local officials said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

With fighting on the front line largely stalled more than 4-1/2 years into the war in Ukraine, Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly struck ​logistics and other economic targets in recent weeks to try to damage the other's war effort.

Russia has for two weeks been carrying out almost constant attacks with faster jet-powered drones that have killed a number of Kyiv residents and disrupted daily life in the capital. The attacks were paused while U.S. peace negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv at the weekend, but then resumed.

"Russia's escalation with jet-powered 'shaheds' is gradually becoming increasingly terrorist in nature," Zelenskiy said on X.

Both sides deny targeting civilians in the war, ‌triggered by Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

ATTACKS ON PETROL ⁠STATIONS

The two dead in Kyiv were at one of the two petrol stations that was attacked, officials said, one by a double-tap strike.

Friday's strikes followed what appeared to be the first attack on a Kyiv petrol station a day earlier. In recent months, ⁠Russia hit some 300 petrol stations, mainly in or near Ukraine's frontline regions.

"There is no military objective behind such strikes. This is terror of the civilian population," said Bohdan Kukura, CEO of Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta.

A further 12 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were injured in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. An attack on a Kyiv residential block injured eight people ​overnight.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Zelenskiy ​said Russia had hit a building used by Ukraine's largest mobile operator Kyivstar in Kyiv, ​and there were strikes in eight other Ukrainian regions. Kyivstar's network ‌continued to operate, the company said.

A woman was killed in the Kyiv region surrounding the capital, the regional governor said.

The governor of Dnipropetrovsk region, Oleksandr Hanzha, said one person was killed and 19 injured in attacks across his region. All but one of the injured were in the city of Dnipro.

A drone attack killed one person in the city of Kharkiv, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. And the Moscow-installed head of Russian-controlled parts of eastern Donetsk region said two local gas company employees were killed in a drone strike.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

ESCALATING STRIKES

Ukraine, in turn, has attacked Russia's largest online retailers and oil refineries, often deep inside the country, as well as energy and ‌fuel logistics in regions of its own territory occupied by Russian forces.

Zelenskiy said Ukrainian forces had ​hit an enterprise and an oil industry facility in the Saratov and Volgograd regions. He also ​reported strikes on unnamed targets in other regions and the Black Sea.

Dmitry ​Milyayev, the governor of Russia's Tula region, said two people had been killed and three injured in Ukrainian drone attacks overnight. A ‌37-year-old man had been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike in ​the Kursk region, its governor said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Russian e-commerce ​company Ozon said a drone had caused a fire at its logistics hub in the central city of Saratov.

Over two dozen warehouses owned by Ozon and fellow online retailer Wildberries have been hit in recent attacks which Kyiv casts as part of a campaign against economic infrastructure underpinning Russia's war ​in Ukraine.

Ukraine's military said it had hit an oil refinery ‌in Saratov.

Two people were injured in a missile attack that hit two residential buildings and damaged an industrial facility in Volgograd, south of ​Saratov on the Volga River, local authorities said, without identifying the industrial facility.

(Reporting by Gleb Garanich in Kyiv, Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo, Anna ​Pruchnicka in Gdansk; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman, Michael Perry, Timothy Heritage and Ron Popeski)

data.title: Oil prices, US inflation stoke Fed hike worries
data.description:
High oil prices, record American diesel costs and hot US inflation data on Friday cemented investor fears that the Federal Reserve is all but certain to hike rates soon, despite the potential to dent growth in the world's biggest economy.

After a rollercoaster week for markets, bonds and energy, driven by a sharp escalation in the US-Iran war, US consumer inflation was unchanged at 3.4 percent in August, in line with analyst expectations -- and well above the Fed's two percent target.

It came a day after the European Central Bank raised eurozone borrowing costs, citing the effects on energy costs from a Middle East conflict that has broadened in the past days following an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

Cresset Capital Management's Jack Ablin pointed to relief that the inflation figures weren't worse.

"It came in as expected," Ablin said. "Investors are resigned to the fact that the Fed is going to raise rates next week."

Yields on long-term US Treasury bonds remained fairly high, but major Wall Street indices won solid gains after four straight negative sessions.

"It's a little frosting on an otherwise rancid cake," Ablin said.

European stocks also closed higher, with Paris and Frankfurt both finishing up 0.8 percent after a volatile week.

Patrick O'Hare, chief market analyst at Briefing.com, however said that "arguably, the market has already been absorbing the likelihood of a rate hike" through the past week's sell-off.

Any increase would put Fed chairman Kevin Warsh on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who has launched an unprecedented campaign against the Fed's independence, demanding policymakers lower interest rates to spur economic activity.

"With the labor market still resilient and monthly core inflation firming, the Fed will find it harder to avoid a hike next week. Markets are pricing around a 90 percent probability, giving policymakers room to act without catching investors off guard," said eToro US Investment Analyst Bret Kenwell.

While oil prices retreated Friday, they remain at levels deemed far too high by central banks hoping to keep inflation pressures from becoming entrenched in the wider economy -- especially with the Houthis cementing their hold on the Bab Al-Mandab strait, a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.

Average diesel prices in the United States climbed above $6 a gallon on Friday for the first time, a shock increase for a key fuel in the transport and agriculture sectors -- and a potential headache for Trump ahead of November's midterms.

Brent oil also almost touched $110 per barrel on Friday, its highest level since May, but fell back after the International Energy Agency slashed its forecast for global oil demand this year, citing the recent escalation in the Middle East war and resurgent energy prices.

Asian stocks slumped across the board in the wake of Thursday's heavy selling, with AI and other heavily indebted tech stocks hit as bond yields soared.

data.title: RFK Jr.'s Wildly Expensive Travel Accommodation Raises Eyebrows
data.description:
RFK Jr.'s Wildly Expensive Travel Accommodation Raises Eyebrows

Curtis M. Wong
Updated Fri, 11 September 2026 at 8:30 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

As Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hits the road to give the Republican Party a boost ahead of the midterm elections this fall, his chosen methods of transportation are raising eyebrows.

A Washington Post report published late Thursday found that Kennedy was granted access to private military aircraft as he travels across the U.S. One such instance, two officials told the outlet, took place Aug. 17, when Kennedy boarded an Air Force-operated Gulfstream jet to fly from Washington, D.C., to Des Moines, Iowa, to attend an event with GOP Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks.

Politics: Secret Service Agent On Leave After Leak About JD Vance's Posh Demands

The Defense Department charges about $9,000 an hour for the use of the Gulfstream jet, when a commercial flight traveling the same distance as Kennedy did that day would cost about $250 for a federal employee.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The White House, as well as lawyers for the Department of Health and Human Services, signed off on the flight arrangements, five people told The Washington Post.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Kennedy's military aircraft use is described as "infrequent," while officials emphasized that the secretary has flown on commercial jets for many of his trips. As the report points out, however, the claims regarding Kennedy's travel are indicative of how Trump has "been more permissive with some Cabinet officials' travel" in his second term.

During Trump's first term, former Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price resigned amid fallout over his use of private jets. Former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and former Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke were also hit with similar controversies, prompting the White House to set new restrictions on Cabinet officials' use of private jets.

Politics: In Keynote Convention Speech, JD Vance Glosses Over Trump Administration's Record

Kennedy, meanwhile, joins a growing list of current Trump officials to draw scrutiny with regard to travel-related requests in recent weeks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A member of the House Judiciary Committee, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), and and Sen. **** Durbin (D-Ill.), who is the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, announced in July that they'd launched an investigation into FBI Director Kash Patel's reported use of public resources for private jets and other travel perks.

That same month, Secret Service supervisors tasked with protecting Vice President JD Vance described many of his requests ― such as the use of a government helicopter to transport him and one of his young sons to a golf lesson ― as "inappropriate or even unprecedented" in an interview with MS NOW.

Vance's office responded to the outlet's report in a statement, which read in part: "While protecting a Vice President with a large policy portfolio and a young and growing family presents a unique challenge, agents of the Secret Service do so with excellence every day."

data.title: Saudi crown prince sought US military help from Trump with Houthis, sources say
data.description:
Saudi crown prince sought US military help from Trump with Houthis, sources say

By Samia Nakhoul, Humeyra Pamuk and Steve Holland
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 8:30 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Samia Nakhoul, Humeyra Pamuk and Steve Holland

ANKARA/WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman sought military assistance from President Donald Trump on Thursday to help fight Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, three sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, as the ‌Houthis stepped up their threat to the Red Sea.

Trump held at least two phone conversations with the Saudi leader on Thursday and did ‌not agree to the U.S. striking Houthis, the sources said. Washington told Riyadh that it would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, they added.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The White House did not address a Reuters question ​on whether there were any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges," the official said.

The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment on the phone calls ⁠and on conversations between the two leaders.

Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for talks, two of the sources said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

News of the request to Trump was first reported by Axios.

SAUDI APPEAL MARKS CHANGE OF ⁠APPROACH

The U.S. war with Iran has entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. The war has driven up prices of global oil and U.S. gasoline, sending Trump's approval ratings to a record low before the November midterm elections.

The Iran-backed Houthis have staged a dramatic advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast in recent days, reaching the ​strategic ​island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Friday, four Yemeni government sources ​told Reuters.

Houthi control of the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, ‌which is on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, could give Iran a critical advantage in its war with the U.S., reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow.

The escalation between the Houthis and Riyadh dates back to early July, when Houthi forces confronted what they said were Saudi warplanes attempting to prevent an Iranian civilian aircraft from landing at Yemen's Sanaa International Airport. ‌That exchange of fire broke a four-year truce in the conflict between the kingdom and ​the Iran-aligned group.

Saudi Arabia told the United States in July that it could fight the Houthis ​on its own and emphasized to Washington that the war should ​not escalate, according to a fourth person familiar with the matter. Saudi officials urged their U.S. counterparts to increase economic ‌pressure on Iran.

A former senior U.S. official familiar with current developments ​said the Saudi leader's Thursday outreach to ​Trump was to see if the U.S. could increase its pressure on the Houthis militarily, instead of Riyadh having to confront the group alone. "So far, they've been told no, but watch that space," the official said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and Iran responded ​with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states ‌that host U.S. bases. U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.

(Reporting by Samia Nakhoul ​in Istanbul and Humeyra Pamuk in Washington, additional reporting by Steve Holland and Jonathan Landay in Washington, Maha el Dahan in Abu ​Dhabi and Bipasha Dey in Bengaluru; Editing by Philippa Fletcher and Timothy Heritage)

data.description:
Brazil's Eduardo Bolsonaro to push for U.S. sanctions against Supreme Court Justice during Washington visit

By Luciana Magalhaes
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 8:08 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Luciana Magalhaes

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Eduardo Bolsonaro, a son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, will renew his push ‌for the United States to reinstate sanctions on Supreme Court ‌Justice Alexandre de Moraes under the Global Magnitsky Act during a Washington visit next week, he ​told Reuters on Friday.

The move comes amid an unusually close election campaign for president in Brazil, where Eduardo's brother Flavio Bolsonaro is statistically tied in run-off polls against incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Eduardo Bolsonaro has been ‌actively promoting his brother's ⁠campaign.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Magnitsky matter itself is something we have been working on for over a year now. So, it is not ⁠an election-related issue," said Eduardo Bolsonaro, declining to disclose details of his agenda during the visit.

The younger Bolsonaro, a former Brazilian congressman, has led a campaign against ​the ​justice, pushing for him to face sanctions ​for his role in overseeing ‌the trial that led to his father's conviction and imprisonment for attempting a coup after losing his 2022 re-election bid.

The Global Magnitsky Act allows the U.S. to impose economic penalties against foreigners it considers to have a record of corruption or human rights abuses. In July of last year, U.S. ‌President Donald Trump sanctioned Moraes, calling the ​trial against former President Jair Bolsonaro a "witch hunt."

Moraes' ​wife was later sanctioned, but ​in December the sanctions were lifted after a diplomatic push ‌by Brazil's government.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, living in ​the U.S. and ​convicted by Moraes in a separate case, now sees room for a reinstatement of the sanctions after an investigation raised suspicions that Moraes ​made improper contact with ‌a banker who allegedly led a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme.

Moraes didn't immediately ​respond to a request for comment.

(Reporting by Luciana Magalhaes, writing by ​Fabio Teixeira; Editing by Aurora Ellis)

WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The contractor responsible for renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington told U.S. President Donald Trump's administration that errors in its work and flaws ‌in the repair plan caused the pool's liner to peel and break loose, the New ‌York Times reported on Friday, citing documents it reviewed.

Trump has repeatedly blamed problems with the newly renovated pool, including its new ​blue paint peeling off, on vandalism.

According to the New York Times, citing the documents, Atlantic Industrial Coatings found problems in the design and execution of the renovation.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Workers did not spray enough primer in some areas, the contractor said in the cited documents, and layers of the liner included incompatible chemicals. The bottom layer blistered and loosened ‌as the chemical on top reached ⁠a hotter temperature than the one underneath could withstand, the New York Times said.

The documents include the contractor's reports to the government and daily progress updates from ⁠the National Park Service over the past two months, the New York Times said.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"President Trump promised to make D.C. safe and beautiful, and he's delivering," said ​Taylor Rogers, ​a White House spokeswoman. "For years, the Reflecting Pool sat ​neglected, plagued with algae, and leaking millions ‌of gallons of water. Fixing it was common sense. It's another example of President Trump restoring our nation's capital for the American people."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A Department of the Interior spokesperson in a statement reiterated that the pool was damaged by vandalism, adding that the contractor was obligated to fix the pool.

"Like any major construction project ... there are always parts of a project where a contractor returns to make sure the work ‌is perfect.

"And in this case, with the major vandalism of ​long razor-blade gashes, the contractor is also replacing the sections ​of the pool damaged by vandals, who ​also repeatedly reached into the pool and ripped at the coating," the spokesperson said.

The ‌Trump administration fast-tracked a renovation of the ​Reflecting Pool ahead of the ​nation's Fourth of July celebrations, at a cost of about $14.7 million.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Within weeks an algae bloom developed and material at the bottom of the pool started peeling off. Federal authorities subsequently charged ​former U.S. Olympian David Hearn and others ‌with vandalism.

But the Justice Department moved to drop the case against Hearn in July, acknowledging ​that the damage to the pool was caused by flawed work performed by the ​renovation contractor.

(Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis, Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)

data.title: Trump’s Aggressive ‘NOT YOU’ Reaction To A Female Journalist Has Experts Seriously Concerned
data.description:
Trump’s Aggressive ‘NOT YOU’ Reaction To A Female Journalist Has Experts Seriously Concerned

Caroline Bologna
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 8:01 pm UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump has a tendency to go after female reporters. On Thursday night, he turned his sights on ABC's Rachel Scott, and body language experts say what happened next was a textbook intimidation display.

Scott pressed Trump about his preposterous promise to send $5,000 checks to every adult citizen in the U.S. if Republicans win the midterm elections.

Life: Trump's Latest 'Unhinged' Attack On A Female Journalist Is 'Quite Alarming,' Experts Say

"If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out to vote?" she asked.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Avoiding the question, the president responded, "I didn't do it for turning out the vote. I did it as a reward for people having to put up with five years and four years of horrible, a horrible situation caused by Biden," he said, later adding. "It's almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden's policies."

When Scott tried to ask a follow-up question about the tariff refund checks Trump had previously promised, he cut her off with "Not you! Not you!" Then, he moved in closer to her face and took on a growling tone as he said, "Hey! Not you!"

"Your network and you, you're the worst," he added.

Life: Trump Was Defensive Over Questions About His MRI — And Experts Say His Body Language Revealed His Go-To 'Tactic'

Traci Brown, a body language expert and behavior analyst, was struck by the physical dimension of Trump's response, particularly the moment he leaned toward Scott.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He is getting on her level, eye to eye, in her face, to threaten and scare her a bit," she told HuffPost.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Rather than let the reporter ask her follow-up question and continue to engage in a back-and-forth dialogue, Trump was "trying to wrestle back control," said clinical psychologist and behavioral expert Denise Dudley.

She identified the president's response as a specific behavioral technique: proxemic intrusion. Basically, it refers to a deliberate violation of personal space used to assert dominance and signal aggression

Life: Trump Yet Again Spat This 1 Insult At A Female Reporter. Experts Say It's A Strategy.

"Proxemic intrusion is an aggressive move, and it's kind of scary to us," Dudley explained. "Human beings and mammals in general are very sensitive to proxemic intrusion because evolutionarily and biologically, we see that as somebody coming in at us and we don't know if they're friend or foe."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Body language and nonverbal communication expert Patti Wood tracked the escalation in Trump's physical behavior, particularly as he moved closer to Scott when she tried to ask a follow-up question.

"His voice rose. He angrily yells at her, 'Hey, not you' the first time, and he steps closer and leans in and repeats with his mouth and lips overworking, overarticulating," she said. "He gives a focused glare of anger with lowered, drawn-together eyebrows."

Then it escalated further. "He moves in closer, leaning in with his full upper body and head closer to her personal zone of space, less than two feet," Wood said. "We see his jaw and chin tighten and his lips thin and tighten. The lips narrowing is a very reliable sign of anger."

Life: Betty Ong Is One Of 9/11's First Heroes. More People Should Know Her Name.

She noted that Trump's anger was not controlled, as his thin lips jutted outward rather than staying closed to contain the emotion.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He singles her out and goes into full attack mode, getting up in her face. His relentless glare of dominance becomes more focused as he attacks, mouth open, upper lip thinning and raised, and teeth showing in a symbolic biting motion as he yells viciously for the third time, 'NOT YOU.'"

Wood also flagged something significant about the duration of the outburst itself.

"Most emotional expressions last very briefly ― two seconds or less in adults, then the adult controls their emotions," she said. "This extended emotional outburst of anger shows his lack of emotional control, which also makes it more frightening."

Dudley also viewed the move as part of a broader strategy.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He's using what we would call multimodal intensification ― a technique where he uses everything at once," she said. "His voice gets louder, and at one point there's a kind of guttural sound that comes in. His movement changes with proxemic intrusion. His gaze gets really intense. And he's pointing, so making a gesture."

Life: A New Study Points To 1 Worrisome Effect Melatonin Could Have On Your Heart Health

On the pointing specifically, Dudley was emphatic.

"Unless you're literally pointing the direction to the bathroom down the hall, you just don't ever point," she said. "Pointing is aggressive. Even though it's your finger, you're pointing a sharp object at somebody, and human beings are sensitive to that."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

These physical changes align with his language and the intensity of his "you're the worst" insult.

"He's definitely exhibiting cluster congruence, or channel congruence," Dudley said. "All the behavioral clusters or channels are saying the same thing. There's no mixed message here. The cluster is congruent. It's verbal and nonverbal signals communicating the same message, which is: I'm done with you, I don't like you, I'm not going to let you keep the floor, and I'm going to go at you."

On the whole, she also sees a menacing vibe to the behavior as well.

"He's pointing and moving in, and the way his face contorts when he leans in, it's threatening," Dudley said. "If somebody leaned in at you and made that face and pointed at you and used that voice tone, you would probably back up. That's what I would do."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Scott did not appear to back up, and both experts found that revealing as well.

"He warned her, waved her off, dismissing her, and she keeps going," Brown said. "That's what reporters do, so there's nothing unusual with her behavior. What is unusual is the stimulus doesn't match the response."

Wood noted the particular vulnerability of Scott's position.

"The attack is full-on and frightening, and what makes it even more frightening is that her position as a journalist and the question she asked were reasonable," she observed. "Just as he has done to other female reporters, he isolates her from the other reporters. She is a female enduring a vicious public attack that she can't defend against or retreat from and keep her job, and no one else comes to defend or protect her. Also, notice she does not sound frightened."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Although Trump has been hostile toward male journalists as well, his attacksonwomenreporters have been particularly brutal ― including calling The New York Times' Katie Rogers "ugly," dismissing CNN's Kaitlan Collins as "very dumb and unhappy," dubbing Maggie Haberman "Maggot Hagerman," telling Bloomberg's Catherine Lucey "Quiet, piggy!" and attacking ABC's Mary Bruce for asking what he called "a horrible, insubordinate, and just a terrible question."

Dudley described Scott's composure in this latest exchange with the president as bravery and professionalism in the face of "aggressive, threatening" behavior.

"This is a good moment for her as a reporter," she said. "The natural response of somebody getting in your face and pointing at you and using that voice tone would be to back up because we as humans sense we're in physical danger. But I would assume that natural response in her is suppressed because her energy and her adrenaline is around getting the story, trying to maintain the floor. And he's trying to get that conversational control away from her."

Additionally, Dudley observed that the president's anger and eruption seemed clearly targeted, rather than general.

"It's not like he's just generally agitated or in a bad mood and mad at all reporters," she said. "When he turns to the next reporter, it's like 'OK, what is your question?' His aggression is aimed right at her. Or he'd be mad at the other guy, but he's clearly not."

data.title: Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races
data.description:
Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races

By Bo Erickson and Dawn Kopecki
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 7:54 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Elon Musk attend a press conference at the White House

1 of 4
U.S. President Donald Trump and Elon Musk attend a press conference in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 30, 2025. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

By Bo Erickson and Dawn Kopecki

NEW YORK, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The two biggest Republican money players in the 2026 midterm elections – U.S. President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk – have finally turned on the spigot with less than eight weeks to go before Election Day.

With Republicans facing the prospect of losing control of at least one ‌chamber of Congress, and polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote, a group connected to Trump has begun spending tens of millions of dollars to reserve blocks of TV ad ‌time in close races.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump, whose approval rating is stuck at the lowest level of his political career, told reporters last week that he planned to allocate $400 million to $500 million to boost Republicans in the midterms.

The Trump-affiliated Republican political action committee No ​Going Back reserved more than $74 million in ad time this week across 15 different House races as well as Senate races in six battleground states: Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, New Hampshire and Ohio, according to political ad research firm AdImpact. More reservations were coming in Friday afternoon, it added.

The PAC has spent the most money, $15.7 million, locking in air time in Michigan where Democratic Socialist Abdul El-Sayed pulled ahead of Republican Mike Rogers in the polls last month, AdImpact said. One of the ads it's airing in that market replays excerpts of interviews with El-Sayed in which he questioned whether police needed to carry guns and ‌called for defunding the police. A spokesperson for El-Sayed didn't immediately ⁠return a request for comment.

Additionally, Musk's America PAC and Trump's main fundraising arm MAGA Inc. have in recent days poured $2.6 million and $10 million respectively into the race for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas where state Attorney General Ken Paxton risks becoming the first Republican to lose to a Democrat in a statewide ⁠election there in decades.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

About $7.1million of that money is being spent on attack ads against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico who leads Paxton by 2.1 percentage points in an average of polls compiled by Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin.

"Republicans now must spend real money defending an expanded map," said Republican strategist Brad Dayspring of Purple Strategies in Alexandria, Virginia. "When you suddenly have to put millions into Texas, having President Trump and Musk open their wallets gives ​Republicans ​the ability to shore up vulnerable races without draining resources from the rest of the map."

Musk's America PAC ​expects to play a major role in Republican voter turnout efforts in key ‌states, with spending on door knockers, digital advertising and direct-mail campaigns ahead of the November 3 election. He's already spent more than $7 million on digital advertising, text messages, voter calls, mailers and other printed materials, federal filings show. A spokesman for the PAC declined to comment.

NEW FUNDRAISING ARM

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump's midterm war chest is supporting the new No Going Back super PAC, according to one person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. It is unclear how much of Trump's war chest will be allocated through this new group.

Though Trump's MAGA Inc. and No Going Back aren't yet formally affiliated with each other, they share the same treasurer – Charles Gantt – phone number and address at the same firm in Massachusetts. Gantt, MAGA Inc. and No Going Back didn't return requests for comment.

It is not clear ‌why the new PAC, which registered with the Federal Election Commission on September 1, was established but Republican strategist ​Ron Bonjean said it helps distance Trump and his MAGA movement from campaign donations as voters sour on the president.

Any ​advertising from the new PAC will be credited to No Going Back PAC instead of ​MAGA Inc., a name closely tied to Trump's political brand.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's a brilliant strategy because it takes MAGA out of the name. It takes any affiliation to ‌Trump out of the name. It has an innocuous name that no one ​will care about as opposed to MAGA Inc., which ​could turn off independent voters right away," said Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions in Washington.

The new PAC has used some of the same vendors as MAGA Inc. to carry out its work and in August some officials from MAGA Inc. started telegraphing to Republicans their intention to create a new PAC, according to the person familiar ​with the operation.

The timing of No Going Back's registration will delay full ‌disclosure of its donors until late October, according to FEC rules.

Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday by proposing ​to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if the party wins the congressional elections. It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would ​be legal.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson in Washington and Dawn Kopecki in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell)
